A B S T R A C T
Knowledge Tracing (KT) plays a crucial role in online education systems, with the primary goal of monitoring
students’ mastery of knowledge during the learning process. Typically, this understanding is assessed through
students’ responses to specific questions. Therefore, the manner in which questions are represented is of
paramount importance in knowledge tracing. Many current KT methods aim to enhance KT by adding
additional features to represent questions. However, this significantly increases the burden and cost of data
collection. Conversely. methods that enhance KT using only basic features (questions and concepts) often
harbor unreasonable assumptions and lack interpretability in representing the questions. Moreover, they fail to
exploit the higher-order relationships between questions, resulting in limited performance. We propose QCKT to
solve these problems. QCKT represents questions from two perspectives. First, by leveraging the relationship
between questions and concepts, question representations were constructed using concept embedding. We
explicitly incorporated the difficulty of questions into this representation to construct interpretable question
representations. Second, to uncover higher-order relationships between questions, we constructed a Concept
Aware Question Relationship Graph and utilize a graph encoder on this graph to aggregate the relationships
between questions. Finally, based on the assumption of different relationship granularities between questions,
we propose five contrastive learning strategies to explore the similarities and differences between these two
types of question representations. We evaluated QCKT by extending 13 existing KT methods to six publicly
available datasets. Extensive experiments demonstrate that QCKT significantly improves the performance, with
many baseline models extended by QCKT exhibiting capabilities surpassing those of state-of-the-art models.

There are several methods [24–26] for this purpose. However, they
often make unreasonable assumptions to simplify tasks. As shown
in Fig. 1, methods such as [24] (Method 1) merge multiple distinct
concepts into a new one to simplify the task, whereas others such as
AKT [25] (Method 2) simplify the task by breaking down multiple
concepts into individual ones. However, neither aligns well with real
educational scenarios. Furthermore, methods such as DHKT [27], and
PEBG [15] often employ random question representations. However,
owing to the vast number of questions, there are limited data on student
responses, making it challenging to optimize the model. Moreover, this
approach lacks interpretability when representing questions. Finally,
they failed to delve deeply into the higher-order relationships among
questions, resulting in constrained performance.
Given the above considerations, it is evident that we must ensure
that questions are associated with multiple concepts (i.e., using the
original data of the unsimplified task). However, we still have the
following challenges to address. First, how do we construct an in-
terpretable question representation? This is crucial, because questions
span the entire process of KT. Second, how do we extract the high-order
relationships between questions? Although graph neural networks offer
a reliable solution, how do we define the graph concerning questions?
Conducting graph neural networks on a complete graph is highly
impractical because it is computationally expensive and weakens the
representation of relationships between similar questions. Finally, we
hope that the final question representation benefits from both aspects.
Contrastive learning [28,29] emerges as a promising solution; however,
it relies on the selection of positive and negative samples. How should
we define positive and negative samples between questions?
To address the challenges mentioned above, in this study, we pro
pose a novel approach called QCKT, which enhances KT by incorporat-
ing an additional Question-based Contrastive learning task. Specifically,
QCKT represents questions from two perspectives. First, by leveraging
attention mechanisms based on the relationship between questions
and concepts, question representations were constructed using concept
embeddings. Inspired by the one-parameter Item Response Theory [30],
which suggests that questions can be distinguished by their difficulty,
we explicitly incorporate question difficulty into this representation to
construct interpretable question representations (the first challenge).
Second, to reduce the number of relationships between the questions,
we utilize concepts related to the questions as premises. In other words,
if two questions contain one or more common concepts, they are
considered related. We refer to the resulting graph under this constraint
as the Concept-Aware Question Relationship Graph and employ a graph
encoder to capture the higher-order relationships between questions
(the second challenge). Finally, to identify positive and negative sam
ples between questions, we propose five contrastive learning strategies
(see Section 4.4) based on the assumption of different granularities
of relationships between questions, aiming to explore the similarities
and differences between questions (the third challenge). We extend
13 existing KT methods to six public datasets to evaluate QCKT, and
extensive experiments demonstrate that QCKT significantly improves
performance. Moreover, many baseline models extended by QCKT show
capabilities that surpass those of state-of-the-art models. We believe
that the simplicity and effectiveness of QCKT will provide new insights
for further KT research.
In summary, our contributions can be summarized as follows:
• <sub>We propose a novel approach, QCKT, that represents questions</sub>
from two different perspectives. This not only effectively captures
high-order relationships between questions but also enhances the
interpretability of question representations.
• <sub>Based on the assumption of different granularities in the rela-</sub>
tionships between questions, we propose five contrastive learning
strategies to uncover the similarities and differences between
questions. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first few at-
tempt at exploring the selection of positive and negative samples
between questions in KT.
• <sub>We extend the 13 KT methods to six publicly available datasets.</sub>
Extensive experiments demonstrate that QCKT significantly im-
proves the performance, and many baseline models extended by
QCKT exhibit capabilities that surpass those of state-of-the-art
models.

2.2. Graph representation learning
Graph Representation Learning (GRL) is a critical field that seeks
to transform graph-structured data into low-dimensional embeddings
while preserving essential structural and semantic relationships. Key
advancements in GRL include methods such as Graph Convolutional
Networks (GCNs) [44], which aggregate information from neighbors
using convolutional operations to capture local structures effectively,
and Graph Attention Networks (GATs) [45], which introduce attention
mechanisms to assign varying importance to neighboring nodes. The
recent GATv2 [46] further enhances this by enabling dynamic attention
coefficients for more expressive modeling. Additionally, methods such
as BGRL [47] leverage contrastive learning objectives to maximize
agreement between positive samples, effectively improving graph rep
resentation quality. Variational approaches, such as the framework
proposed in VCLANC [48] integrate structural and attribute informa
tion through variational inference, enabling effective representation
and clustering of attributed networks by capturing both node attributes
and graph topology. Together, these advancements highlight GRL’s ver-
satility and its potential to tackle challenges in understanding complex
relationships, uncovering latent patterns, and driving innovation across
various applications.
2.3. Question representation in KT
The KT process primarily relies on students’ responses to ques-
tions, emphasizing the significance of questions throughout the KT pro
cess. Therefore, the representation of these questions is of paramount
importance.
Given the importance of textual content in question representation,
EERNN [17], EKT [16], and RKT [18] utilize word2vec [49] to rep-
resent questions based on textual information. By contrast, qDKT [14]
employs FastText [50] to represent questions based on their order of
arrangement.
Inspired by graph neural networks, research on mining question rep
resentations from question-based graphs has increased. Methods such
as DHKT [27] and PEBG [15] transform the relationship between ques-
tions and concepts into constraints, constraining question representa-
tions using the relationships between questions themselves. CoKT [51]
utilizes node2vec [52] on a heterogeneous graph of questions, concepts,
and students to explore the relationships between questions and other
entities. GIKT [53] employs GCN [44] on a bipartite graph of questions
and concepts to represent questions. Bi-CLKT [54] constructs question-
question and concept-concept graphs based on answer accuracy to
mine question information. �<sup>2</sup>-HHN [19] defines heterogeneous graphs
of various entities (e.g., questions, templates, students and topics) to
represent questions.
Unlike others, QCKT does not rely on additional features (such
as question text content or question templates) and only requires
questions and concepts. Additionally, to delve deeper into question
representations, we approach them from two distinct perspectives: one
based on the relationship between questions and concepts, combined
with question difficulty, for an interpretable representation, and the
other from a graph perspective to uncover higher-order relationships
between questions. Furthermore, based on the assumption of different
relationship granularities between questions, we propose five con-
trastive learning strategies to explore these relationships. Additionally,
we extensively expand upon numerous KT methods on multiple public
datasets, with extensive experiments consistently demonstrating the
effectiveness of QCKT. This suggests that QCKT can easily augment
other KT methods to enhance their performance, a capability lacking
in most KT approaches.

as DHKT [27] and PEBG [15] transform the relationship between ques-
tions and concepts into constraints, constraining question representa-
tions using the relationships between questions themselves. CoKT [51]
utilizes node2vec [52] on a heterogeneous graph of questions, concepts,
and students to explore the relationships between questions and other
entities. GIKT [53] employs GCN [44] on a bipartite graph of questions
and concepts to represent questions. Bi-CLKT [54] constructs question-
question and concept-concept graphs based on answer accuracy to
mine question information. �<sup>2</sup>-HHN [19] defines heterogeneous graphs
of various entities (e.g., questions, templates, students and topics) to
represent questions.
Unlike others, QCKT does not rely on additional features (such
as question text content or question templates) and only requires
questions and concepts. Additionally, to delve deeper into question
representations, we approach them from two distinct perspectives: one
based on the relationship between questions and concepts, combined
with question difficulty, for an interpretable representation, and the
other from a graph perspective to uncover higher-order relationships
between questions. Furthermore, based on the assumption of different
relationship granularities between questions, we propose five con-
trastive learning strategies to explore these relationships. Additionally,
we extensively expand upon numerous KT methods on multiple public
datasets, with extensive experiments consistently demonstrating the
effectiveness of QCKT. This suggests that QCKT can easily augment
other KT methods to enhance their performance, a capability lacking
in most KT approaches.

In this section, we analyze the validity of the difficulty learned by

5.9.2. Application
The most interesting application of knowledge tracing may be to
trace students’ knowledge states. Once a student’s knowledge mastery
is accurately captured, teachers can provide targeted tutoring to help
them. Fig. 7 shows the evolution process of tracing a student’s knowl
edge state using DKT + QCKT. Specifically, we randomly selected a
student from the ASSIST09 dataset who answered five questions in 25
time steps. As shown, when the student answers a question correctly
or incorrectly during practice, their mastery of the question clearly
strengthens or weakens, respectively. Moreover, as time passes, we find
that the student gradually forgets questions he/she have previously
mastered. Additionally, as the number of practice questions increased,
the traced knowledge states became more stable. Overall, the stu-
dent’s final knowledge state significantly improved compared to the
beginning, even though he/she answered some questions incorrectly.
This is consistent with our intuition that practicing questions benefits
students’ knowledge mastery, and even answering questions incorrectly
can enhance knowledge.

7. Limitation and future work
Although the question representation learned by QCKT has the
potential to significantly enhance other KT methods, it relies on as-
sociated concepts, a dependency prevalent in nearly all current KT
methods. This paper has made some efforts to address this issue, such
as the calculation of

inclusion of strategy
, which does not involve any concepts; however,
this is insufficient. Overcoming the reliance on concepts for question
representation constitutes the most significant limitation of QCKT and
is a major deficiency of current KT approaches.
We believe that the use of fewer features, such as eliminating
concepts, to advance KT is a promising direction. This approach re-
lies heavily on unsupervised learning and data enhancement methods.
However, in KT, unsupervised learning is still in the early stages of
research, and the means of data enhancement are limited. Classic data
enhancement methods, such as GAN [71], VAE [72] and MAE [73],
have not been thoroughly explored for KT. Introducing them into KT is
still an unexplored area. We hope to delve deeper into these directions
in future work, aiming to solve the issue of concept dependency in
question representations and provide more innovative solutions.
